title: BALAAM WAS HIRED TO CURSE ISRAEL—BUT EVERY TIME HE OPENED HIS MOUTH, GOD TURNED THE CURSE INTO A BLESSING
paragraphs: BALAAM WAS HIRED TO CURSE ISRAEL—BUT EVERY TIME HE OPENED HIS MOUTH, GOD TURNED THE CURSE INTO A BLESSING

They paid a prophet to destroy a people God had chosen. They built altars, offered sacrifices, and searched for a place where the curse might finally work. But there was one terrifying problem for Israel's enemies: No amount of money could make God betray His own word. And hidden inside this ancient confrontation is a warning about compromise, a revelation about grace, and a breathtaking glimpse of Jesus Christ.
There is something deeply unsettling about discovering that someone has been speaking against you behind your back.
Especially when you have done nothing to deserve their hatred.

Imagine people discussing your downfall while you are sleeping. Imagine someone hoping your marriage collapses, your ministry fails, your children wander, or your future never becomes what God intended.
You are going about your ordinary life, completely unaware that somewhere else, people are discussing how to bring you down.
Now imagine something even more astonishing.
Every time they attempt to pronounce destruction over you, God intervenes.
Every time they prepare a curse, blessing comes instead.
Every time they try to overturn what God has spoken, they discover that heaven is not for sale.
That is not merely a comforting thought.
Something remarkably similar happened in the wilderness thousands of years ago.
And the people who were being targeted did not even know the full story unfolding above them.
But before we celebrate the blessing, we need to understand the danger.
Because this story contains a truth that many Christians desperately need to hear.
An enemy may fail to curse what God has blessed, yet temptation can still lead God's people into devastating compromise.
And that is where the story of Balaam becomes far more personal than most people realize.
Israel had come out of Egypt.
They had witnessed the Red Sea open. They had eaten manna in the wilderness. They had experienced God's provision, correction, mercy, and faithfulness.
But they were not a perfect people.
They complained. They doubted. They rebelled. They repeatedly struggled to trust the very God who had rescued them.
Still, the Lord had not abandoned His covenant purposes.
Now they were camped in the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho.
And King Balak was terrified.
Numbers 22:3 tells us that Moab was exceedingly afraid because Israel was numerous.
Balak had seen what happened to other kings who stood against Israel.
He knew he could not afford to treat this people lightly.
So instead of beginning with an ordinary military strategy, he sought a supernatural advantage.
He sent messengers to a man named Balaam, son of Beor.
Balaam had a reputation.
People believed that whoever he blessed would be blessed, and whoever he cursed would be cursed.
Balak wanted that reputation working for him.
His request was direct.
“Come now therefore, I pray thee, curse me this people; for they are too mighty for me.” — Numbers 22:6, KJV
There it was.
A king wanted a curse.
A diviner was offered a reward.
And an entire nation was the target.
But the first extraordinary moment came before Balaam ever reached Moab.
God spoke.
And God's answer was unmistakable.
“Thou shalt not curse the people: for they are blessed.” — Numbers 22:12, KJV
Read those words again.
For they are blessed.
Not because Israel had never sinned.
Not because they had earned an exemption from discipline.
Not because every Israelite was spiritually mature.
They were blessed because God had made covenant promises, and His purposes could not be purchased away by a frightened king.
In the original Hebrew, the final words are:
כִּי בָרוּךְ הוּא — ki varukh hu
Literally, “for it is blessed,” referring collectively to the people.
The word barukh comes from the Hebrew root associated with blessing.
And the force of the statement is extraordinary.
God was not inviting Balaam to decide whether Israel deserved blessing.
God was announcing a reality Balaam had no authority to reverse.
What God had declared was not Balaam's to sell.
That should confront something in us.
Because how often do we live as though another person's opinion possesses more authority than God's word?
Someone rejected you, and you began calling yourself worthless.
Someone betrayed you, and you started believing you were unlovable.
Someone spoke against your future, and suddenly you feared that their words could cancel everything God might still do in your life.
But Balaam's story exposes the limits of human power.
People can lie about you.
They can oppose you.
They can wound you.
They can create real consequences through their actions.
But they cannot bribe God into becoming unfaithful to His promises.
And for those who belong to Jesus Christ, the foundation of hope is even greater than Israel's experience in Moab.
It is the finished work of the cross.
But we are not there yet.
Because Balaam's heart was already being tested.
When the first messengers returned without him, Balak refused to accept defeat.
He sent more distinguished officials.
He promised greater honor.
He offered Balaam the possibility of extraordinary reward.
And here the story becomes uncomfortable.
Balaam already knew what God had said.
He had been told not to curse Israel.
Yet the offer of reward remained before him.
He entertained the delegation again and sought further direction.
Numbers 22:20 records that God permitted Balaam to go under a strict condition: he could speak only what God commanded.
Yet Numbers 22:22 immediately tells us that God's anger was kindled as Balaam went.
The narrative creates a deliberate tension.
Permission to travel was not permission to pursue greed, manipulate divine instruction, or curse God's people.
The New Testament later helps us understand the moral danger in Balaam's story.
Peter describes Balaam as one “who loved the wages of unrighteousness” (2 Peter 2:15, KJV).
Jude speaks of the error of Balaam for reward.
And suddenly this is no longer just a story about an ancient diviner.
It is a mirror.
Because sometimes the most dangerous temptation is not something we openly call evil.
Sometimes it is something we desperately want, even after God has made His will clear.
A relationship we keep justifying.
A dishonest opportunity that promises financial relief.
A compromise we describe as necessary.
A secret habit we keep defending.
A decision we continue reconsidering because obedience would cost us something we do not want to surrender.
We may know what Scripture says.
We may even be able to quote it.
But knowing God's word and loving God's will are not always the same thing.
And then comes one of the strangest scenes in the entire Bible.
Balaam is riding his donkey.
The angel of the LORD stands in the road with a drawn sword.
Balaam cannot see him.
But the donkey can.
Three times the animal turns away from danger.
Three times Balaam becomes frustrated.
And eventually, in his anger, he strikes the donkey.
Then something extraordinary happens.
“And the LORD opened the mouth of the ass.” — Numbers 22:28, KJV
The donkey speaks.
And Balaam answers.
It is almost impossible to read the scene without noticing its irony.
A man sought for his supposed spiritual insight cannot see the danger directly in front of him.
An animal sees what the prophet cannot.
The man who is supposed to speak powerful words needs to be corrected through the mouth of a donkey.
And when God finally opens Balaam's eyes, he sees the angel standing with a sword drawn.
The angel explains that the donkey's actions had spared Balaam's life.
Think about that.
The very thing Balaam was striking had been protecting him.
The delay he resented had been mercy.
The obstruction that frustrated him had kept him from destruction.
How many times have we become angry at something that may have been restraining us from a terrible decision?
Not every closed door is divine intervention.
Not every inconvenience carries a hidden spiritual message.
We must be careful not to pretend we know God's secret purposes behind every disappointment.
But Scripture does show us here that Balaam misjudged the very thing God used to spare him.
And that should make us humble.
Sometimes we are far less perceptive than we imagine.
Sometimes our desires have become so loud that correction sounds like interference.
Sometimes we are willing to fight against anything standing between us and what we want.
Even when what we want is destroying us.
Balaam confessed his sin and offered to turn back.
Yet he was instructed to continue, speaking only what God gave him.
And so he finally arrived before Balak.
The king had waited.
The payment had been promised.
The confrontation was about to begin.
Balak took Balaam to a place overlooking part of Israel's camp.
Altars were prepared.
Sacrifices were offered.
Seven bulls and seven rams were presented.
The king expected a curse.
But when Balaam opened his mouth, the words were not what Balak had purchased.
“How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed? or how shall I defy, whom the LORD hath not defied?” — Numbers 23:8, KJV
Imagine Balak hearing that.
He had summoned a man to weaken his enemy.
Instead, the man publicly acknowledged that he could not overturn God's verdict.
Balak was furious.
“What hast thou done unto me? I took thee to curse mine enemies, and, behold, thou hast blessed them altogether.” — Numbers 23:11, KJV
But Balak did not give up.
He changed the location.
Perhaps another vantage point would produce a different result.
Perhaps a new arrangement of sacrifices would finally bring the answer he wanted.
Perhaps the problem was the place.
So they tried again.
And once more, the blessing prevailed.
Then came one of the most powerful declarations in the entire account.
“God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?” — Numbers 23:19, KJV
The Hebrew begins:
לֹא אִישׁ אֵל וִיכַזֵּב — lo ish El vikhazzev
“God is not a man, that He should lie.”
The point is not that God never responds to human repentance or never changes an announced course of judgment. Scripture contains examples of God showing mercy when people turn from evil.
The point here is that God is not fickle, deceitful, or vulnerable to manipulation like a human being.
He does not abandon His covenant faithfulness because someone offers enough money.
He does not become a liar because a king becomes desperate.
He does not revise His character to satisfy Balaam's ambition.
And then Balaam declares:
“Behold, I have received commandment to bless: and he hath blessed; and I cannot reverse it.” — Numbers 23:20, KJV
I cannot reverse it.
There are words you need to stop allowing to govern your identity.
The insults spoken over your childhood.
The shame attached to your past.
The rejection you have carried for years.
The accusations that convinced you redemption was impossible.
None of those things should be treated as more authoritative than what God says through Jesus Christ.
But understand this carefully.
Numbers 23 is not a promise that Christians will never suffer, never face opposition, or never experience the consequences of sin.
Israel itself would experience severe judgment for disobedience.
The message is not that belonging to God makes us untouchable by pain.
The message is that God's covenant faithfulness cannot be overturned by human manipulation.
And in Christ, our confidence rests not in our circumstances, but in the Savior who has reconciled us to God.
Balak tried a third time.
Another location.
Another arrangement of altars.
Another expectation.
But Numbers 24 tells us that Balaam no longer went searching for omens as before.
The Spirit of God came upon him.
And once again, blessing came forth.
“How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, and thy tabernacles, O Israel!” — Numbers 24:5, KJV
Consider the scene.
Below the heights lay Israel's camp.
Ordinary families.
Children.
Elders.
People preparing food, tending animals, carrying burdens, and facing the uncertainties of wilderness life.
They did not know everything being said about them from the mountains.
They did not hear every conversation between Balak and Balaam.
Yet God was defending His covenant purposes.
There is something profoundly comforting in knowing that God's faithfulness does not depend on our awareness of every danger.
But do not miss what happens next.
Because the story does not end with a triumphant slogan about every curse becoming a blessing.
It becomes darker.
And the warning is devastating.
Balak finally loses patience.
He tells Balaam to flee.
He had promised honor, but now declares that Balaam will receive none.
Before leaving, Balaam delivers further prophetic messages, including a remarkable announcement concerning Israel's future.
“There shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel.” — Numbers 24:17, KJV
In Hebrew, the phrase includes:
דָּרַךְ כּוֹכָב מִיַּעֲקֹב — darakh kokhav mi-Ya'aqov
“A star shall come forth from Jacob.”
And:
וְקָם שֵׁבֶט מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל — veqam shevet mi-Yisra'el
“And a scepter shall arise from Israel.”
The star and scepter are royal images.
In the immediate ancient setting, the oracle speaks of a future ruler arising from Israel who will defeat hostile powers, including Moab.
Within the larger biblical story, Christians have long understood this royal hope in relation to the Messiah, Jesus Christ, the promised Son of David.
We should not flatten every detail into a simplistic prediction, but neither should we ignore the trajectory of Scripture.
God's redemptive purposes were moving toward a King greater than any earthly ruler.
And that King would not merely defeat political enemies.
He would confront humanity's deepest enemies: sin, death, and the power of darkness.
But before we reach Bethlehem and Calvary, there is a terrible event in the wilderness.
Numbers 25 records that Israel began engaging in sexual immorality with Moabite women and participating in sacrifices to their gods.
Israel was drawn into idolatry.
The people whom Balaam could not successfully curse were now falling into grievous sin.
And Numbers 31:16 later identifies Balaam's counsel as a factor in the Peor incident.
Revelation 2:14 confirms the connection, describing Balaam as one who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before Israel, leading them into idolatrous eating and sexual immorality.
That changes how we understand the entire story.
Balaam could not make God curse Israel.
But Scripture later connects him with counsel that enticed Israel into unfaithfulness.
What the attempted curses could not accomplish, compromise brought into the camp.
And that should sober every believer reading this.
Because the enemy does not always need to destroy your faith through open persecution.
Sometimes temptation is enough.
Not because Satan is stronger than Christ.
Not because God's grace is fragile.
But because sin is deceitful, and the human heart can become dangerously skilled at making disobedience appear harmless.
We can resist obvious opposition while quietly entertaining the very habits that weaken our devotion.
We can reject false accusations while refusing to confess genuine sin.
We can celebrate God's promises while treating His commandments as optional.
We can talk about spiritual warfare and neglect the ordinary call to holiness.
And sometimes the greatest danger is not the person speaking against us.
It is the compromise we have welcomed into our own lives.
Perhaps that is why this story hurts.
Because many of us know what it means to survive an attack from outside and then stumble through a decision made in private.
You resisted the criticism.
You endured the rejection.
You survived the betrayal.
But when temptation came dressed as comfort, acceptance, pleasure, or relief, you stopped resisting.
And now you carry a regret you cannot easily explain.
A secret you have been hiding.
A season of compromise you wish you could erase.
A prayer you have struggled to pray because you feel too ashamed to look toward heaven.
And perhaps you have begun believing the worst thing you did is now the truest thing about you.
But listen carefully.
The God who refuses to be manipulated by Balaam is also the God who takes sin seriously enough to provide a Redeemer.
That is where the Gospel enters this story with breathtaking clarity.
Because we must not confuse God's covenant blessing with permission to sin.
And we must not confuse His judgment against sin with the absence of mercy.
Israel's failure at Peor was real.
The consequences were devastating.
God did not pretend idolatry was harmless.
And He does not ask us to pretend our sins are harmless either.
But the Bible does not end with Israel's rebellion.
It moves forward through centuries of promise, failure, judgment, mercy, and longing.
Until the promised King comes.
Jesus Christ.
The One who never compromised with sin.
The One who never needed to be corrected for greed.
The One whose obedience was complete.
The One who did not merely speak about God's faithfulness but embodied it perfectly.
And here the story reaches its deepest reversal.
Balaam was hired to speak a curse, but God compelled him to speak blessing.
At Calvary, the sinless Son of God willingly bore the curse of the law on behalf of sinners.
Paul writes:
In the original Greek:
Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου
Christos hēmas exēgorasen ek tēs kataras tou nomou.
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law.”
The verb exēgorasen expresses redemption or release by purchase.
And the word katara refers to a curse.
Paul is not describing an imaginary curse cast by a jealous neighbor.
He is speaking of the real condemnation associated with transgression of God's law.
And his announcement is astonishing.
Jesus redeemed us from that curse.
Not by pretending we were innocent.
Not by declaring our rebellion unimportant.
Not by bribing divine justice.
But by giving Himself for us.
The innocent Christ suffered for the guilty.
The righteous Savior died for the unrighteous.
The One who deserved no condemnation endured the cross so that sinners might receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
And that is why the Gospel is infinitely greater than a message about escaping negative words.
The greatest problem in our lives is not that somebody might curse us.
It is that we have sinned against a holy God.
And the greatest blessing is not that everyone who opposes us will fail.
It is that Jesus Christ has opened the way for guilty people to be forgiven, justified, adopted, and made new.
Paul continues in Galatians 3:14 by connecting Christ's redemption to the blessing of Abraham coming to the Gentiles through Jesus Christ and the promised Spirit being received through faith.
Do you see how beautiful this is?
The blessing promised through Abraham reaches its fulfillment in Christ.
The nations are invited into the promise through faith.
And what no human diviner could manufacture, God gives freely through His Son.
This is not cheap grace.
It cost Jesus His life.
And it does not leave us unchanged.
It calls us to repent.
To turn from sin.
To abandon the idols we have been defending.
To stop calling darkness harmless.
To surrender the secret places where compromise has taken root.
And to trust the Savior who died and rose again.
Maybe you have been living like Balaam.
You know the right words.
You know the language of faith.
You can recognize Scripture when you hear it.
But there is something you have been unwilling to release because the reward seems too attractive.
Maybe you have been living like Israel at Peor.
God has shown you mercy again and again, yet you have been giving your heart to things that compete with Him.
Or maybe you are simply exhausted.
You have been wounded by other people, ashamed of your own failures, and frightened that you have wandered too far to come home.
If that is you, hear the invitation of Jesus.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because His mercy is sufficient for all who come to Him.
You do not have to clean up your entire history before turning toward Christ.
You come to Him in repentance and faith.
You confess what is true.
You stop defending what is destroying you.
And you trust the One whose blood is sufficient to cleanse sinners.
The cross is where our excuses die.
But it is also where hope is born.
The resurrection declares that death did not have the final word.
And in Christ, neither must your past.
That does not mean every consequence disappears.
Some broken relationships take time to heal.
Some wrongs require restitution.
Some wounds require patient care, accountability, and support.
But forgiveness is real.
Restoration is possible.
And the Holy Spirit truly transforms those who belong to Christ.
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior has always carried the words:
Not because God pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because every painful chapter receives the ending we would have chosen.
But because Jesus can redeem sinners whose stories seemed hopeless.
He can take the proud and teach them humility.
The greedy and teach them generosity.
The compromised and lead them into repentance.
The wounded and sustain them through healing.
The guilty and give them forgiveness.
The spiritually dead and make them alive.
And perhaps the most unforgettable part of Balaam's story is this:
A king spent his resources trying to purchase a curse.
But the blessing of God could not be bought.
And centuries later, the King of kings purchased our redemption with something infinitely more precious than silver or gold.
His own blood.
Peter writes that believers were redeemed not with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19).
Balak's money could not overturn God's word.
Balaam's ambition could not rewrite God's covenant.
And our money cannot purchase salvation either.
Grace is not for sale.
It never was.
It never will be.
That truth matters especially in a world where even religious messages can sometimes make people feel that God's love depends on how much they give.
It does not.
You cannot purchase forgiveness through an offering.
Jesus Christ alone saves.
And because He saves freely, our generosity can become something beautiful: not a payment for grace, but a grateful response to it.
This ministry exists to keep proclaiming Christ, encouraging repentance, strengthening believers, and making biblical truth accessible to people who may be struggling silently.
Every article shared, every prayer offered, every resource distributed, and every person reached matters.
And continuing and expanding that work requires faithful support.
Think of it as a voluntary, recurring ministry offering—an opportunity to participate in the work of sharing the Gospel and supporting ongoing discipleship.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, not pressured.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
It is simply a meaningful way to help sustain this particular ministry.
And if you are unable to give financially, you are no less welcome here.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
These items can serve as everyday reminders of the truth we proclaim, but they are never the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
And our deepest desire is not merely that people wear a message.
It is that they live transformed by the Savior behind that message.
Because spiritual nourishment should never be reserved only for those who can afford to pay.
We want people to open their Bibles.
To examine the Scriptures.
To recognize false teaching.
To understand the Gospel.
To grow in holiness.
To learn how to pray.
To endure suffering with faith.
To find biblical encouragement in difficult seasons.
And above all, to know Jesus Christ more deeply.
But there is another way you can help this message travel farther than you may ever know.
Not merely because you enjoyed reading it.
But because someone in your circle may be living under the weight of condemnation.
Someone may be terrified that their past has destroyed their future.
Someone may be compromising their faith while telling themselves they are still spiritually safe.
Someone may have mistaken a season of discipline for proof that God no longer welcomes the repentant.
And someone may desperately need to discover that the Gospel offers something greater than a temporary feeling of encouragement.
It offers reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
Send it privately to someone who needs hope.
Invite seekers.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite people who have questions about Jesus.
Even invite those who do not yet believe, because the Gospel is not afraid of sincere questions.
And if you have been reading this with a heavy heart, I want to ask you something personal.
Not for appearances.
Not to impress anyone.
But because sometimes spiritual honesty begins when we finally stop pretending.
Where are you in this story?
Are you afraid of what others have spoken against you?
Are you struggling to trust what God has said?
Are you fighting a temptation you have not told anyone about?
Or have you been carrying the shame of a compromise you desperately want to leave behind?
You do not have to disclose private details publicly.
“Jesus, teach me to trust Your Word and turn from compromise.”
And if Christ has already brought you through a season of repentance and restoration, consider sharing a brief testimony.
Your story may encourage someone who believes change is impossible.
We are not here to glorify our failures.
We are here to glorify the Savior who rescues sinners.
And before you leave this article, I want you to return with me to that hillside in Moab one final time.
Picture the king standing beside Balaam.
The sacrifices have been offered.
The altars are behind them.
The nation of Israel lies below.
The king has money, influence, ambition, and fear.
The diviner has a reputation and the opportunity for reward.
Everything has been arranged for a curse.
And then Balaam opens his mouth.
But the words refuse to obey the king's desire.
Because there is a throne higher than Balak's.
An authority greater than Balaam's reputation.
A promise no human payment can purchase or destroy.
And a God who remains faithful to His word.
Yet Israel's later compromise reminds us that being the object of God's covenant purposes was never a license to abandon holiness.
The blessing was real.
The warning was real.
The consequences of sin were real.
And so was God's continuing redemptive purpose.
That is why we must not walk away from this story merely shouting, “No one can curse me!”
We must walk away asking a deeper question.
Am I trusting the God who keeps His promises, while also surrendering the sins that are drawing my heart away from Him?
Because the greatest victory is not merely surviving the hostility of others.
It is belonging to Jesus Christ.
It is knowing that your sins have been forgiven through His blood.
It is being reconciled to the Father.
It is receiving the Holy Spirit.
It is learning to walk in truth when compromise would be easier.
It is refusing to sell your obedience for temporary reward.
It is discovering that the grace which welcomes repentant sinners also teaches them to leave their former ways behind.
And if today you recognize yourself in Balaam's greed, Israel's compromise, or the fear of those who feel surrounded, do not turn this moment into another excuse to hide.
Come to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Trust His finished work.
Receive His mercy.
And follow Him.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that your choices never mattered.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ is mighty to save sinners who could never save themselves.
The cross does not call evil good.
It reveals the terrible cost of sin and the immeasurable love of the Savior.
And the empty tomb declares that the crucified Christ is alive.
So do not let this be another article that stirs your emotions for a moment and leaves your life unchanged.
Open your Bible.
Read Numbers 22 through 25.
Read Numbers 31:16.
Read 2 Peter 2, Jude, and Revelation 2:14.
Then read Galatians 3 and see how the Gospel reveals the fullness of God's redemptive promise in Christ.
Ask the Lord to expose whatever you have been justifying.
Ask Him for the courage to obey.
Ask Him to make you faithful when the reward for compromise appears attractive.
And ask Him to give you a heart that loves Jesus more than the approval, wealth, pleasure, or acceptance of this world.
Not because Christ needs your money to remain King.
But because the King has graciously allowed His people to participate in making His name known.
The God who could not be bribed by Balak is still worthy of our wholehearted worship.
The Savior who bore the curse for sinners is still worthy of our complete surrender.
And the risen Christ is still transforming lives that the world may have already written off.
One final thought.
Balak wanted the last word over Israel.
Balaam wanted the reward.
Israel needed mercy more than it realized.
And humanity needed a Redeemer far greater than Balaam could ever have imagined.
That Redeemer has come.
His name is Jesus.
And when you stand before Him, the question that matters most will not be whether everyone spoke well of you.
It will be whether you belong to the One who died and rose again to save sinners.

The most astonishing reversal was never that Balaam could not pronounce a curse over Israel—it was that Jesus willingly bore the curse we deserved so that, through faith in Him, we could receive the blessing we could never earn.
